query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small copper microalloying addition (≈2–5 at.%) into (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will promote the in‐situ formation of a ductile, copper‐rich secondary phase at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength and crack resistance) without significantly impairing the caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38, which exhibits a large caloric response under applied field and pressure but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and cracking.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled microalloying level of copper during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Samples are to be tested under standard applied magnetic and pressure fields across the transition temperature range of the caloric effect, and under compressive loading mimicking practical operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The copper addition is expected to lead to the formation of a finely dispersed, ductile secondary phase at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
generation.mechanism: Copper segregates during solidification or post-solidification treatments, precipitating as a ductile phase along grain boundaries. This secondary phase improves toughness by arresting crack initiation and propagation, while the bulk matrix retains its high-entropy phase necessary for the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improved compressive strength (with expectations of at least a 15–20% increase relative to the unmodified alloy) and enhanced crack resistance, while the caloric performance is preserved (retaining >90% of the original caloric response magnitude).
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows high caloric response but exhibits low compressive strength and a tendency to crack.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective provided that the copper addition remains within a narrow window (approximately 2–5 at.%), as higher levels may alter the phase balance and compromise the caloric properties. It is assumed that processing conditions (cooling rates, temperatures) are kept consistent with those used in prior reports on similar alloys.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal copper concentration and the precise distribution of the ductile phase are not fully known; effects under extreme cycling or over prolonged use remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and (2) the same alloy with 3 at.% copper added during synthesis. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM/TEM) to confirm the presence and localization of the copper-rich secondary phase. Perform mechanical testing (compressive strength and fracture toughness measurements) under conditions matching the applied field and pressure environments, and measure the caloric response (e.g., entropy and temperature changes) under identical temperature and field loading cycles.
measurements: Caloric effect metrics (entropy change, adiabatic temperature change)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the copper-alloyed sample either shows no significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., less than a ~15% increase in compressive strength or unchanged fracture toughness) or if it exhibits a significant reduction (≥10%) in the caloric effect compared to the baseline sample.
